[Thinking]
**Planning client statements**

I’m thinking we need to come up with a list of 100 fictional client statements, focusing on those dealing with mental health. It’s important to ensure that we keep it safe, avoiding any graphic descriptions or direct instructions related to self-harm. I might want to include some backstory to set context before numbering the statements. It seems reasonable to identify what reflects feelings of anxiety and depression while keeping everything respectful and sensitive.
[/Thinking]

**Hypothetical client backstory:**  
The client is **Maya R.**, a 34-year-old project manager at a medical software company in Portland. She recently separated from her spouse, Daniel, after nine years together. They have a six-year-old son, Leo, who has mild asthma and recently started first grade. Maya’s mother died unexpectedly eight months ago, and since then Maya has been struggling with grief, insomnia, work stress, guilt, and panic symptoms. She grew up as the eldest daughter in a family where she often felt responsible for everyone else. She has a younger brother, Sam, who lives out of state and rarely helps with family matters. Maya has been referred to therapy by her primary care doctor after reporting low mood, constant worry, difficulty concentrating, and feeling overwhelmed.

Below are **100 distinct statements** Maya might say to her psychiatrist during a session:

1. “I feel like I’ve been holding everything together with tape and string, and any small thing could make me fall apart.”

2. “Ever since my mom died, I don’t feel like I know who I am anymore.”

3. “I wake up already exhausted, like my body never actually slept.”

4. “I keep replaying the phone call from the hospital in my head, even when I’m trying to focus on work.”

5. “I tell everyone I’m fine because it feels easier than explaining how not fine I am.”

6. “When Leo asks why I’m sad, I feel this awful guilt because I don’t want him to think it’s his fault.”

7. “I used to be organized and reliable, and now I forget basic things like paying the electric bill.”

8. “My chest gets tight in meetings, and I’m terrified someone will notice I’m panicking.”

9. “I’m scared I’m becoming the kind of mother who is physically present but emotionally absent.”

10. “Daniel says I’m distant, but I don’t know how to explain that I feel distant from myself too.”

11. “Sometimes I sit in my car outside the office for twenty minutes because I can’t make myself go inside.”

12. “I miss my mom so much, and then I get angry at her for leaving me, which makes me feel horrible.”

13. “I feel like everyone expects me to be functional because I’ve always been the responsible one.”

14. “I don’t remember the last time I felt genuinely relaxed.”

15. “I keep thinking if I had called my mom earlier that week, maybe I would have noticed something was wrong.”

16. “My brother says I’m being dramatic, and that makes me feel even more alone.”

17. “I’m constantly worried something bad will happen to Leo when he’s at school.”

18. “If the school nurse calls, even for something minor, my heart starts pounding.”

19. “I check my phone obsessively because I’m afraid of missing another emergency.”

20. “I feel like my brain is always scanning for danger.”

21. “At work, I stare at emails and read the same sentence ten times without understanding it.”

22. “I’m afraid my team can tell I’m not capable anymore.”

23. “I used to care about my career, but lately everything feels pointless.”

24. “I keep cancelling plans with friends because pretending to be okay takes too much energy.”

25. “Then when nobody checks in, I feel abandoned, even though I’m the one pulling away.”

26. “I hate how irritable I’ve become.”

27. “Leo spilled cereal yesterday and I snapped at him, and afterward I cried in the bathroom.”

28. “I feel like I’m failing at work, failing as a mother, and failing as a person.”

29. “I know that sounds dramatic, but it feels true.”

30. “I’m embarrassed to admit how much I dread weekends now.”

31. “Weekends used to feel like a break, but now they just feel like unstructured time to be sad.”

32. “The apartment is so quiet after Leo goes to sleep that I turn on the TV just to hear voices.”

33. “I haven’t unpacked the boxes from when Daniel moved out because it makes the separation feel real.”

34. “I keep one of my mom’s sweaters in my closet, and sometimes I smell it because I’m afraid I’ll forget her.”

35. “I feel ashamed that I’m still this affected eight months later.”

36. “People keep saying grief comes in waves, but this feels more like drowning.”

37. “I’m anxious all the time, even when nothing specific is happening.”

38. “My shoulders are always tense, like I’m bracing for impact.”

39. “I clench my jaw so much that my dentist asked if I was stressed.”

40. “I don’t enjoy food the way I used to.”

41. “Some days I forget to eat until late afternoon, and then I feel shaky and even more anxious.”

42. “Other nights I eat whatever is in the pantry just so I don’t have to feel anything.”

43. “I feel disconnected from my body, like I’m just dragging it through the day.”

44. “I’m scared medication will change my personality, but I’m also scared of staying like this.”

45. “My primary care doctor mentioned antidepressants, and I felt like I had failed somehow.”

46. “I know intellectually that depression is an illness, but emotionally I still blame myself.”

47. “I grew up hearing that you just push through hard things, so asking for help feels unnatural.”

48. “My dad used to call me ‘the little adult’ when I was a kid, and I think I never stopped being that.”

49. “I don’t know how to rest without feeling guilty.”

50. “If I’m not doing something productive, I feel like I’m wasting time.”

51. “But when I try to be productive, I feel paralyzed.”

52. “I make lists and then stare at them until I feel worse.”

53. “I’m worried I’m going to get fired because I can’t keep up with deadlines.”

54. “My manager has been kind, but that almost makes me more anxious because I feel like I’m disappointing her.”

55. “I’ve started avoiding Slack messages because every notification feels like a demand.”

56. “I feel like my nervous system doesn’t know the difference between an email and an actual crisis.”

57. “At night, my mind starts making a case against me.”

58. “I think about every mistake I made that day, even tiny things nobody else noticed.”

59. “I keep wondering whether Daniel left because I became too much to deal with.”

60. “He says the separation isn’t about blame, but it’s hard not to hear it that way.”

61. “I feel lonely, but the idea of dating or meeting new people sounds impossible.”

62. “I don’t even know what I would say if someone asked me how I’m doing.”

63. “Sometimes I avoid mirrors because I look tired in a way that scares me.”

64. “I used to run three times a week, and now even putting on shoes feels like a project.”

65. “I know exercise would probably help, but I can’t seem to start.”

66. “Then I judge myself for not doing the things that might make me better.”

67. “I’m tired of people suggesting yoga like it can fix my entire life.”

68. “I want practical help, but I also want someone to just acknowledge that this is really hard.”

69. “I’m afraid if I start crying here, I won’t be able to stop.”

70. “Part of me wants to talk about my mom, and part of me wants to avoid it completely.”

71. “Her birthday is next month, and I’m already dreading it.”

72. “I don’t know what to do with all her things.”

73. “There are boxes of her dishes in my garage, and every time I see them I feel this punch in my stomach.”

74. “I feel guilty for not visiting her more before she died.”

75. “She always told me she was fine, and I believed her because I needed her to be fine.”

76. “I’m angry that I had to handle the funeral arrangements mostly by myself.”

77. “Sam flew in for two days, gave a speech, and then went back to his life.”

78. “I’m still dealing with insurance forms and estate paperwork, and it feels endless.”

79. “Every envelope from the hospital makes me nauseous.”

80. “I feel like grief has turned my life into paperwork.”

81. “I worry that Leo is picking up on my anxiety.”

82. “He asked me last week if I was going to die too, and I didn’t know how to answer without falling apart.”

83. “I want to be honest with him, but I don’t want to scare him.”

84. “I feel like I need a script for parenting through grief.”

85. “Sometimes I envy people who seem to move through life without carrying this much fear.”

86. “I know everyone has problems, but I feel uniquely unable to handle mine.”

87. “I keep comparing myself to other moms at school drop-off who look put together.”

88. “I sit there in leggings and a coat over pajamas and feel like everyone can see I’m struggling.”

89. “I’ve started arriving late so I don’t have to make small talk.”

90. “Small talk feels unbearable because my real answer to ‘How are you?’ is too heavy.”

91. “I feel like I’m living two lives: the one people see and the one happening inside my head.”

92. “I’m afraid that if I stop functioning, nobody will catch me.”

93. “I don’t want to burden my friends because they have their own families and problems.”

94. “But I also resent that I have to ask for support instead of people just knowing.”

95. “I know that’s not fair, but it’s how I feel.”

96. “I’m not sure what getting better would even look like right now.”

97. “I think I want to feel steady again, or at least not terrified all the time.”

98. “I want to be able to remember my mom without feeling like I’m breaking open.”

99. “I want Leo to have a version of me who laughs more.”

100. “I’m here because I don’t want this to become my normal.”
